text:
Philip Rubin is a prominent figure in computational psychology and speech technology. He earned a BA in psychology and linguistics from Brandeis University and a PhD in experimental psychology from the University of Connecticut under the supervision of Michael Turvey, Ignatius Mattingly, Philip Lieberman, and Alvin Liberman. His research spans the fields of embodied cognition, speech production, and speech perception, with a focus on the biological bases of speech and language.
Rubin is best known for his foundational work in articulatory synthesis, including the development of the ASY and SWS systems—programs that model the physiology and acoustics of speech production. He introduced the concept of speech gestures, which describe and control articulatory events, and developed the configurable articulatory synthesizer (CASY), a 3D model of the vocal tract that allows researchers to simulate and analyze speech production. He also contributed to the development of the TADA system, which models inter-articulator coordination and gesture dynamics.
In addition to his work in speech synthesis, Rubin has made significant contributions to the theoretical understanding of speech and perception, particularly through his work on the dynamics of speech production and perceptual organization. He is recognized for his dynamical systems perspective on speech, emphasizing the spatiotemporal coordination of articulatory movements and the role of embodied systems in shaping speech.
Rubin has held leadership roles in science administration and policy, including serving as Director of the Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences at the National Science Foundation (NSF) and as Assistant Director for Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP). He has also been a key figure in science policy, serving on the National Academies Board on Behavioral, Cognitive, and Sensory Sciences, and the Board of the Federation of Associations in Behavioral and Brain Sciences (FABBS).
He is a strong advocate for ethical considerations in research and emerging technologies, particularly in relation to human subjects and the use of technology by intelligence and law enforcement agencies. He has served on advisory committees related to human research protections and has been involved in efforts to improve transparency and oversight in research practices.
Rubin is a member of several prestigious organizations, including the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the American Psychological Association, and the American Association for the Advancement of Science. He has received numerous awards, including Fellowships from the Acoustical Society of America, the American Psychological Association, and the American Psychological Society, and the National Medal of Science.
His work has been widely recognized and has influenced the development of both speech technology and cognitive science. He continues to be active in research, education, and policy, and is currently the President of the Federation of Associations in Behavioral and Brain Sciences (FABBS).
